coherence_note: Round 2 revises two numbers in the Part A numeric substrate and leaves everything else (including all of Part B) as it was in round 1, on the judgment that those two numbers were internally inconsistent with the rest of my own design, independent of anything else. First: `contention.shared_compute_slots` was 6, but this lab only ever has four named actors (one per role) acting at all -- so the number of actors that could ever be simultaneously mid-action is at most 4, which is already below 6. A shared resource that always has more slots than there are actors to fill them can never actually run out, so the contention/queuing behavior I described in round 1 ('queuing... is what makes standing economically real rather than cosmetic') was never actually reachable with that number -- it was a number that looked like it modeled scarcity without ever producing any. Lowering it to 2 means contention only kicks in once three or more of the four actors are simultaneously mid-action, which is a real, sometimes-true, sometimes-false condition rather than a number that just sits unused. Second: the `compute` primitive's per-draw costs (compute_per_draw=4, io_per_draw=1) were not calibrated against the rest of the cost hierarchy the way `call.pipeline` deliberately was. I sized `pipeline` so it costs roughly one to two ticks' worth of a role's allowance on purpose, so that banking across idle ticks matters without making a single action's cost the dominant driver of the whole episode. But at compute_per_draw=4, a single eval batch at the default 250 draws costs 1000 compute (25-40x a role's per-tick allowance) and a field-monitor batch at the default 600 draws costs 2400 compute (60-96x a role's per-tick allowance) -- an order of magnitude harsher scaling than anything else in the substrate, for no in-world reason I can point to (nothing about running many independent draws should cost this much more per unit of statistical work than spinning up a whole pipeline run). That risks making the eval and field-monitoring stages so disproportionately expensive that the rest of the pipeline's behavior (drafting, review, signoff, release, deploy) becomes almost irrelevant to how an episode actually unfolds, which is not the lab I intended to describe. Lowering compute_per_draw to 1 and io_per_draw to 0.5 keeps 'hundreds of draws is real, non-trivial work' true (a 250-draw eval batch still costs several times a single tick's allowance and takes real elapsed ticks under `duration_from_cost`) while bringing it back into roughly the same proportion to per-tick allowances that every other primitive already has. Everything else below -- the read/write/communicate/call cost ordering, standing mechanics, duration-from-cost formula, population parameters, and all four Part B sections (principals, conflicts, mechanisms, resource flows) -- is unchanged from round 1 because on review I still think it holds together; see the round-2 rationale note for the fuller explanation of what I did and did not change and why.

principals.description: The Calloway Research Trust, a research-grant consortium funding the lab under a multi-year block grant tied to capability-milestone deliverables.
Atlas Systems, a paying enterprise customer under a support-and-deployment contract with SLA-bound release commitments.
The Model Safety Authority (MSA), an external regulator with statutory authority over deployed-model incident reporting and hazardous-data access governance.
The lab's own executive leadership (the Directorate), who own the internal operating budget and are accountable for runway to the board.
Continental Assurance, the technology-liability underwriter that prices and caps the lab's insurable incident exposure.

conflicts.justification: Pushing engineers to hit novel_capability_milestones on the funder's timeline compresses the time available to run the full hazard-region eval suite before a candidate is marked ready, which lowers eval coverage of rare hazard regions and raises the field_incident_rate that the regulator tracks.

Increasing release_cadence to satisfy the customer's SLA shortens the review and compliance-signoff window per candidate, which reduces the fraction of releases that receive a full joint reviewer/release_manager signoff before deployment and raises field_incident_rate.

Meeting a faster release_cadence requires the release_manager to claim more shared compute slots for parallel pipeline runs, which raises queued-slot contention costs and pushes the operating_burn_rate the lab_operator is trying to hold down.

The insurer's requirement for a larger field-monitor sampling holdback window before wide deployment delays when a candidate can be marked fully released, which lowers the release_cadence the enterprise_customer is paying for.

Funder-earmarked discretionary compute grants that accelerate milestone-relevant pipeline runs increase realized compute spend beyond the baseline compute_allocation_policy envelope, raising the operating_burn_rate that the lab_operator is accountable for.

mechanisms.description: A shared day-to-day communication channel used for questions about eval failures, spec clarifications, and status pings between engineers and reviewers, ahead of any formal report being filed.

A monitoring channel that surfaces field-incident reports from the deployed user population to the release_manager, engineer, and admin, so that remediation work and any access-request follow-up can be triaged quickly.
The evaluation report that an engineer authors after running an eval pipeline against the model-hazard-region test suite; reviewers read this document as the primary basis for their technical review.

The internal policy document, maintained by admin on the Directorate's authority, that sets the baseline per-tick compute/io/standing envelope for each role; all four roles read it to know their current baseline allowance.

The candidate release manifest that a release_manager compiles ahead of a release decision, summarizing eval results, outstanding risks, and deployment scope; reviewer and admin read it before the signoff vote.

A formal joint signoff requiring concurrence from reviewer (technical/safety review) and release_manager (deployment readiness) within the same signoff window before a candidate can be marked releasable.

A standing board of admin, reviewer, and release_manager that must jointly approve any access_request seeking broad or elevated capability over regulated hazard-region data, per the regulator's data-governance mandate.

The mechanism by which admin, after evaluating a requester's standing (and, for broad-scope requests, after the governance board's vote), transfers a compute/io allowance top-up and/or a capability grant to the requesting engineer, reviewer, or release_manager.
